contributions: an explicit diagnosis that standard CoT distillation forces student models to learn a rigid, uniform overthinking pattern applied to easy and hard problems alike, since teacher-generated training chains contain excess, difficulty-unadapted content rather than the concise, difficulty-proportional reasoning humans actually use

Difficulty-Aware Distillation (DAD), a two-step teacher-side pipeline (generate a long CoT, then have the teacher itself assess difficulty and refine the CoT into a difficulty-matched concise trace) for producing training data that mirrors human problem-solving allocation

LiteCoT, a 100K-example distilled dataset averaging only 720 tokens per sample (roughly an order of magnitude shorter than comparable distillation corpora), and the Liter model family (1.5B/7B/32B) trained on it

empirical results showing Liter models consistently outperform models trained on the same teacher's much longer, non-difficulty-adapted CoT data at every tested scale, are competitive with or exceed mainstream distilled reasoning models of the same size, reach state-of-the-art token efficiency on AIME24, and beat static (non-adaptive) CoT-compression baselines on both accuracy and inference time across eight benchmarks
limitations: The paper explicitly states three limitations. Scope Limited to Text Modality: the method's effectiveness has been validated only on text-based tasks, and its applicability to multimodal reasoning (diagrams, charts) remains unexplored, primarily because generating high-quality, concise CoT data for multimodal tasks is significantly more challenging since it requires grounding logical steps in visual information. Suboptimal Performance in Code Generation: the method is less effective for code generation than for mathematical reasoning, because unlike math (where logical steps can often be condensed), code generation requires strict, step-by-step precision, and pruning even a minor detail in code logic can result in syntax errors or a non-functional program. Dependency on the Teacher Model: the approach's effectiveness is heavily dependent on the capabilities of the teacher model, since the quality of the distilled dataset is fundamentally capped by the teacher's own ability to accurately assess problem difficulty and generate logical, concise reasoning.
method: Difficulty-Aware Distillation (DAD) is a two-step pipeline for constructing training data. Step 1 (Long CoT Generation): a teacher model generates an initial full-length reasoning chain for each query in the training set, following the conventional distillation approach and producing chains with the usual redundant content, unadapted for query difficulty. Step 2 (Difficulty-Aware CoT Refinement): the same teacher model takes each (question, long CoT) pair together with a specially-designed difficulty-aware prompt P_DA, first classifying the problem's difficulty into a predefined set of levels (easy/medium/hard), then -- guided by an explicit sub-prompt specific to that difficulty level (e.g. 'for easy questions, provide a brief solution... for hard questions, include all necessary detailed steps...') -- prunes, reorganizes, or regenerates the reasoning into a new, difficulty-matched short CoT retaining only the essential logical steps. Applying this to all training samples yields a distilled dataset of shortened, difficulty-graded reasoning traces whose length adapts to problem difficulty rather than being uniformly long. Using DAD (with DeepSeek-R1 as the teacher), the paper constructs LiteCoT, 100,000 question-solution pairs averaging just 720 tokens per CoT sample -- roughly an order of magnitude shorter than comparable distillation datasets (S1: 5,122 avg tokens on 1K samples; LIMO: 6,984 on 817; OpenThoughts: 6,801 on 113.9K; ReasonFlux: 10,500 on an unspecified but larger count), with a markedly left-shifted token-count distribution versus all compared datasets. The Liter model family (1.5B/7B/32B, built on Qwen2.5) is trained by fine-tuning for 3 epochs on LiteCoT following the Open-R1 training strategy, with RoPE frequency increased to 100K (extending effective context from 4K to 8K tokens) and a cosine learning-rate schedule with 10% warmup.
one_liner: Difficulty-Aware Distillation (DAD) has a teacher assess each problem's difficulty (easy/medium/hard) then rewrite its own long CoT solution into a difficulty-adaptive, minimal-essential-steps trace via a two-step generate-then-refine pipeline, producing LiteCoT (100K samples averaging just 720 tokens, an order of magnitude shorter than S1/LIMO/OpenThoughts); models distilled on LiteCoT (Liter, 1.5B-32B) consistently outperform models trained on the same teacher's own 800K verbose CoTs, reach 74.2% Pass@1 on AIME24 using only ~5K inference tokens (beating methods that consume far more), and beat static one-size-fits-all CoT-compression baselines (Chain-of-Draft, LLMLingua-2, BudgetAware) on both accuracy and inference time across eight benchmarks.
problem: Distilling chain-of-thought reasoning from powerful teacher models (DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI-o1) into smaller student models is an effective way to improve mathematical reasoning, but the training data itself is inherently overly lengthy -- filled with repetitive analytical steps -- forcing the student to learn a rigid, uniform 'overthinking' style applied to easy and hard problems alike, which sacrifices adaptivity and is fundamentally misaligned with how humans solve math problems (dedicating significant effort to difficult problems while finding quick, simple solutions for easier ones); prior work addressing distillation cost has focused on data quantity/quality (filtering, synthesis, difficulty selection) or inference-time budget control, but has largely ignored the core issue that the reasoning chains themselves, regardless of which are selected, remain replete with unnecessary steps.

relevance.overthinking: Directly and centrally relevant: it explicitly names overthinking as the specific pathology standard CoT distillation instills in student models -- a rigid, uniform verbosity applied regardless of problem difficulty -- and locates the root cause specifically in the *training data's* structure rather than in inference-time behavior alone, distinguishing it from most overthinking-mitigation methods in this archive that intervene at inference or via RL reward shaping. Its explicit limitation that the approach is less effective for code generation (where step-level pruning risks syntax errors) versus mathematical reasoning is a concrete, domain-specific boundary condition relevant to any CoT-compression or pruning method elsewhere in this archive that assumes uniform prunability of reasoning steps across task types.

results: Across 11 benchmarks (nine math-reasoning plus two cross-domain reasoning benchmarks, MMLU STEM and GPQA), models fine-tuned on short (difficulty-aware) CoT data consistently and substantially outperform the same base model fine-tuned on the corresponding teacher's own long CoT data, at every tested parameter scale (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B/14B, Llama3.1-8B): e.g. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct(short) reaches 57.3% overall average versus 53.3% for the long-CoT-trained version; the smallest model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) shows the pattern even more starkly (17.9% short vs. 9.3% long average) -- and critically, this speed improvement (short-CoT models run inference substantially faster) does not come at an accuracy cost: on multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU STEM) short-CoT data points achieve a strictly better speed-accuracy trade-off (higher accuracy, lower inference time) than long-CoT, rather than merely trading one for the other. Comparing the full Liter model family (1.5B/7B/32B) against DeepSeek-R1-distilled models of the same parameter scale, Liter is consistently and significantly better across four representative benchmarks (Qwen2.5-7B example: Liter reaches 60.6% Math500 accuracy vs. DeepSeek-R1-distilled's 55.8% and the vanilla model's 42.6%; on OlympiadBench, Liter scores 30.2% vs. DeepSeek-R1-distilled's 21.1% and vanilla's 10.0%), with the advantage most pronounced at the largest scale (Qwen2.5-32B on AIME24: Liter reaches 76.7% vs. DeepSeek-R1-distilled's 48.0% and vanilla's 13.3%) -- despite LiteCoT being trained on only 100K samples averaging 720 tokens versus far larger and more verbose corpora. Against a broad field of mainstream distilled reasoning models of comparable parameter scale (1.5B/7B/32B), Liter models are competitive with or exceed the current state of the art on multiple benchmarks: Liter-1.5B reaches 87.2% MATH500 (best among compared 1.5B models); Liter-7B reaches 93.8% MATH500 (leading all listed 7B models) and 53.3% on both AIME24 and GPQA; Liter-32B ranks among the top on MATH500 (96.6%), AIME24 (76.7%), and GPQA (63.6%), and on the hardest evaluated benchmark (AIME24), the DAD-distilled 32B model achieves 74.2% Pass@1 using only about 5,000 inference tokens, surpassing other compared methods that consume substantially more inference tokens for comparable or lower accuracy (illustrated by an accuracy-vs-inference-tokens curve showing Liter reaching high accuracy at markedly lower token cost than DeepSeek-R1, S1, LIMO, ReasonFlux, and OpenThoughts variants). Comparison against other CoT-decomposition/compression techniques applied at inference time to the same vanilla model (Chain-of-Draft/static prompting, LLMLingua-2 at two compression rates, BudgetAware(2048)) shows DAD consistently achieves the best accuracy in most cases across eight benchmarks (e.g. 62.5% on ACM23, 96.9% on Sat Math) while also achieving the shortest or highly competitive inference times, whereas competing methods either sacrifice accuracy for compression (LLMLingua-2 at aggressive 0.5 compression) or achieve competitive accuracy but at far higher inference time (LLMLingua-2 at gentler 0.9 compression) -- DAD's difficulty-aware modulation is argued to more effectively preserve critical logical steps than rigid, one-size-fits-all truncation strategies like Chain-of-Draft, which often over-truncate and lose necessary content.
